content: 1. Gatifloxacin is the fluoroquinolone most likely to cause dysglycemia, while moxifloxacin is the least likely. Dysglycemia may manifest as either hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia. Use caution and monitor blood glucose levels when administering quinolone antibiotics, especially in patients with diabetes or those on insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents. Moxifloxacin can enhance the effects of insulin glargine, insulin glulisine, insulin lispro, insulin NPH, and regular human insulin through pharmacodynamic synergy, necessitating close monitoring. 2. Moxifloxacin increases the effects of metformin, miglitol, nateglinide, pioglitazone, rosiglitazone, saxagliptin, and sitagliptin via pharmacodynamic synergy, potentially leading to hypoglycemia. Gatifloxacin is more likely to cause dysglycemia compared to moxifloxacin. Monitor blood glucose levels closely in patients receiving these combinations. 3. Administration of quinolone antibiotics, including moxifloxacin, with corticosteroids (e.g., methylprednisolone, prednisone, prednisolone, mometasone) may increase the risk of tendon rupture. Use caution and monitor patients closely, particularly those with predisposing factors such as advanced age or a history of tendon disorders. 4. Moxifloxacin and other drugs that prolong the QTc interval (e.g., lapatinib, lenvatinib, leuprolide, methadone, mifepristone, osilodrostat, osimertinib, oxaliplatin, paliperidone, paroxetine, pasireotide, pazopanib, quetiapine, quinine, quizartinib, ranolazine, rilpivirine, risperidone, romidepsin, selpercatinib, sorafenib, sulfonamides, telavancin, triclabenazole, trimethoprim, triptorelin, tropisetron, valbenazine) may have additive effects on QTc prolongation, increasing the risk of torsades de pointes and other ventricular arrhythmias. ECG monitoring is recommended, and therapy should be modified or alternative agents considered if necessary. 5. High doses of fluoroquinolones, including moxifloxacin, in combination with NSAIDs (e.g., ketoprofen, ketorolac, meloxicam, nabumetone, naproxen, oxaprozin, piroxicam, sulindac, tolmetin) or other CNS-stimulating agents (e.g., meclofenamate, mefenamic acid) may increase the risk of CNS stimulation and seizures. Use caution and monitor closely. 6. Moxifloxacin may decrease the efficacy of oral hormonal contraceptives (e.g., levonorgestrel, ethinyl estradiol, mestranol) by altering intestinal flora. Although the risk of contraceptive failure is low, additional contraceptive measures may be considered. Monitor for potential interactions. 7. Moxifloxacin levels may be reduced by cation-containing products (e.g., lanthanum carbonate, magnesium chloride, magnesium citrate, magnesium hydroxide, magnesium oxide, magnesium sulfate, magnesium supplements, sucralfate, sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid, sodium sulfate/potassium sulfate/magnesium sulfate, trimagnesium citrate anhydrous). These agents inhibit gastrointestinal absorption of moxifloxacin. To avoid chelation, administer moxifloxacin at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after these agents. 8. Moxifloxacin may decrease the levels or effects of phenytoin and sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid by unknown mechanisms or altered metabolism. Monitor closely for therapeutic efficacy and adjust therapy as needed. 9. Moxifloxacin may increase the toxicity of rilpivirine, triptorelin, and other QTc-prolonging agents, raising the risk of torsades de pointes. Use caution, monitor ECGs, and consider alternative therapies if available. 10. Moxifloxacin may increase the effects of repaglinide and other antidiabetic agents, potentially leading to hypoglycemia. Monitor blood glucose levels closely and adjust antidiabetic therapy as needed. 11. Moxifloxacin may increase the toxicity of valbenazine and other QTc-prolonging agents. Use caution, monitor ECGs, and modify therapy as necessary to minimize the risk of arrhythmias.
